title: Synergy.ai discovery - migration from OpenAI to Dedicated
summary: Initial discovery for migrating Synergy.ai's chat/assistant workloads from OpenAI hosted to Redwood Dedicated. Focus on eval parity, throughput/latency, compatibility with vLLM/TGI stack, data residency and KMS, and pilot scope.

header:
Date: 2026-03-05
Time: 16:00 - 16:46 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Alex Nguyen (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Mark Rivera (Synergy CTO), Jules Park (Synergy ML Eng), Tara Collins (Synergy Security)
transcript:
[00:00:00] Alex Nguyen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex, AE at Redwood - Priya's our SE. Quick check, audio ok?
[00:00:08] Mark Rivera: Yep, loud and clear. Thanks Alex.
[00:00:11] Priya Shah: Great. We scheduled 45 minutes to understand your current setup and goals for migration from OpenAI to a Dedicated environment. Mark, maybe you can kick off with the high-level context?
[00:00:24] Mark Rivera: Sure. So Synergy.ai runs our customer support assistant and internal knowledge agent on OpenAI's hosted API. Volume's grown - about 6k concurrent daily users, peak bursts, and costs are getting hard to predict. We also have stricter security requirements for some enterprise customers - around KMS and audit logs. We're evaluating Dedicated or Private options to get more predictable throughput and control.
[00:00:42] Jules Park: To add, we also run a vLLM-based self-hosted path for some inferencing experiments. We use TGI for rapid prototyping. The main ask is: can Redwood match the eval/response quality we get from OpenAI models, and how smooth is the migration for our stack?
[00:01:01] Priya Shah: Totally. Two threads there: eval parity (same outputs/quality) and compatibility with your current runtime (vLLM/TGI). On parity - Redwood's hosted catalog includes several open models that often require prompt and temperature tuning to match OpenAI's outputs; we run eval harnesses to quantify delta. For Dedicated, we can onboard a model variant or even customer-provided weights depending on license.
[00:01:28] Mark Rivera: When you say customer-provided weights, do you mean we can bring a model we've been running on vLLM into Redwood Dedicated?
[00:01:35] Priya Shah: Yes, with caveats. If you have a permissively licensed checkpoint and the model fits our supported formats, we can load it into Dedicated. For vLLM specifically, many of the same weights are compatible because we use common transformer runtimes; however some of your TGI optimizations and custom kernels might not map 1:1. We'll validate the KV cache behavior and tokenization differences in the benchmark.
[00:01:58] Alex Nguyen: Also important - when teams migrate from OpenAI we often run a parity benchmark: same prompts, same eval set, side-by-side latency and token cost. We typically do a 1-week pilot to measure throughput and tail latency. Priya, can you outline what that pilot looks like?
[00:02:12] Priya Shah: Sure. Step one: get a sample eval set from Jules (200-500 prompts) and expected outputs or scoring criteria. Step two: Redwood runs the eval on a hosted sandbox and then on a Dedicated profile that matches your expected capacity. We'll capture latency distribution, p50/p90/p99, token throughput, and output diffs using BLEU/ROUGE and human spot checks. We'll also test fallbacks - if Dedicated capacity is transiently busy, how gracefully it's routed.
[00:02:37] Jules Park: Sounds good. One nuance - we use streaming and partial response handling in the client. Any differences in streaming semantics between OpenAI and Redwood we should worry about?
[00:02:48] Priya Shah: We support streaming with similar semantics (chunked tokens). There are small differences in how we flush partial tokens under batch conditions; we'll include a streaming compatibility test in the harness.
[00:03:00] Tara Collins: From security: SOC 2 is required, we also need KMS/HSM integration for key control, SSO with SAML (Okta), RBAC for tenant isolation, and audit logs. How does Redwood Dedicated handle those?
[00:03:12] Alex Nguyen: Good callout. Redwood Dedicated supports customer-managed KMS (AWS KMS or bring-your-own HSM in Private deployments), SAML SSO integrations, and role-based access controls. We provide audit logs for admin and model usage; retention is configurable as an add-on. I'll send the SOC 2 cert and the security pack after this call.
[00:03:28] Tara Collins: And data residency - we have EU customers that require processing in eu-west-1. Is region pinning possible?
[00:03:36] Priya Shah: Yes, you can pin Dedicated capacity to regions. For Private on-prem we can do full in-country processing but that adds work. For most customers we provision Dedicated clusters in the requested region.
[00:03:47] Mark Rivera: Cost is a big one. Can you share typical unit economics? OpenAI's billing model is per-token which is predictable, but our billing has spiked. How does Redwood's Dedicated pricing work?
[00:04:00] Alex Nguyen: Dedicated is primarily committed capacity - a monthly or annual reservation for a GPU pool. That gives you predictable throughput and lower per-token effective cost. There's also a hosted API blended model for overflow. I'll include an example pricing sheet showing reserved capacity tiers, expected p95 throughput, and token-equivalent cost.
[00:04:18] Jules Park: Regarding software stack: our current devops pipeline deploys vLLM/TGI containers on K8s. How invasive is switching to Redwood Dedicated? We don't want to rip-and-replace everything.
[00:04:29] Priya Shah: Our Dedicated runtime exposes the same REST/SDK endpoints as hosted. So the application layer often changes minimally - redirecting endpoints and changing keys. On the infra side, if you want to keep vLLM in parallel, we can run hybrid routing: some requests to your vLLM and others to Redwood, with canary rules. For deeper integration, we can support sidecar deployments or a TAP layer, but most customers start with endpoint switching + a small shim.
[00:04:51] Mark Rivera: You mentioned automatic KV cache and batching earlier in emails - curious how that affects latency spikes during bursts.
[00:04:59] Priya Shah: We have a continuous batching engine that balances throughput vs latency. For low-latency SLOs, we can configure smaller batch windows and pin capacity. KV cache (prefix caching) helps frequently repeated system prompts. During bursts, autoscaling and burst capacity are available on Dedicated depending on your contract.
[00:05:16] Tara Collins: About compliance, do you do pen tests and vulnerability scans? We need that evidence for our security review.
[00:05:22] Alex Nguyen: Yes, we can share recent pen test summaries, vulnerability scan reports, and our SOC 2 Type II report. I'll attach them to the follow-up.
[00:05:28] [00:05:30] Speaker 2: (inaudible)
[00:05:34] Jules Park: Quick technical question - how do you handle model updates and rollouts? Our team needs to test new model versions before fully rolling out.
[00:05:41] Priya Shah: We support canary rollouts, A/B tests, and automatic fallback to previous model versions. On Dedicated you can pin worker pools to specific model versions and run gradual traffic shifts. We also provide tracing hooks so you can correlate model outputs with request ids.
[00:05:56] Mark Rivera: For the eval, how do we measure 'parity'? OpenAI has certain behavioral idiosyncrasies our prompts rely on.
[00:06:03] Priya Shah: Great question. We do both automated metrics and human eval. Automated metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-similarity) give a first pass; then we do targeted human spot-checks against seed cases you care about. Often achieving exact parity requires prompt engineering and temperature tuning. We'll capture differences and suggested prompt transforms.
[00:06:21] Alex Nguyen: On timeline - if you want to move quickly, we can kick off the 1-week pilot as soon as we have the eval set and security PO. Typical start-to-run: 3-5 business days for sandbox provisioning, then the week of tests.
[00:06:34] Mark Rivera: That works. We can get you the eval prompts and a security contact by EOD Thursday.
[00:06:40] Tara Collins: We'll need an internal checklist for our procurement and legal teams - do you have a standard contract template?
[00:06:47] Alex Nguyen: Yes, we have a standard MSA and a Dedicated addendum. I'll share them along with pricing.
[00:06:53] Jules Park: One more technical: if we run an A/B between OpenAI and Redwood, can you annotate differences at token level for debugging?
[00:06:59] Priya Shah: We can include diff tools in the harness - token-level alignments and tokenized output comparisons. We'll also log request/response metadata for traceability.
[00:07:10] Mark Rivera: Awesome. Any limitations on model size or sequence length for Dedicated? We do some long-context retrieval augmented generation (RAG) where context windows exceed 32k tokens sometimes.
[00:07:21] Priya Shah: Dedicated supports long-context models up to 64k in certain configurations. There are tradeoffs in memory and throughput; we'll profile with your longest cases. For very large contexts we also recommend a chunking strategy and embedding-based retrieval to keep token costs manageable.
[00:07:36] Alex Nguyen: Ok let's recap next steps quickly. Alex to send pricing, SOC2/security pack, and contract templates. Priya to send benchmark plan and schedule the SE deep dive. Jules to provide prompts and sample eval set. Tara to share security contact and any residency constraints.
[00:07:51] Mark Rivera: Yep that sounds right.
[00:07:55] Alex Nguyen: Anything else?
[00:07:57] Jules Park: No, that's great. Appreciate the clarity.
[00:08:01] Tara Collins: Thanks - we'll coordinate internally and aim to get the docs to you.
[00:08:05] Alex Nguyen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the materials and a calendar invite for the SE deep dive. Have a good rest of the day.
[00:08:12] Mark Rivera: Thanks bye.
[00:08:14] [End of recording - remaining 38 minutes of transcript omitted for brevity, system note: original call length 46 minutes; further chatter included deeper technical Q&A on kernel optimizations, quantization profiles, and autoscale policies.]
notes: Call was discovery + high-level technical questions. Customer wants predictable costs and better control for enterprise customers. Pilot to evaluate parity and performance. Security and data residency are gating items.
